parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bürküt (“Burkut; eagle”). Exact source unknown, possibly Chagatai [script needed] (börküt) or Kazakh бүркіт (bürkit), or Tatar бөркет (börket). Compare also Bashkir бөркөт (börköt), Kyrgyz бүркүт (bürküt), Uzbek burgut.
From Old Chuvash *våtaɣ, *uotaɣ, from Proto-Turkic *ōtag. The sense developed from “tent, family” to “group of people”. Compare Turkish otağ (“tent”).

Borrowed from a Turkic language, from Proto-Turkic *kiayguk (“boat, oar”). Compare Azerbaijani qayıq (“boat”), Crimean Tatar qayıq (“boat”), Kyrgyz кайык (kayık, “boat”), Southern Altai кайык (kayïk, “oar”), Turkmen kayık (“boat”), Uzbek qayiq (“boat”). Doublet of каи́к (kaík).

From Proto-Turkic *kïŕïl (“red”). Thoroughly replaced the native Slavic word (дёрен (djóren) from *dernъ) early as also with Belarusian кізі́л (kizíl), while Ukrainian дере́н (derén) is still more common than кизи́л (kyzýl). Compare Ottoman Turkish قزلجق and Turkish kızılcık (cornelian cherry).
Likely from the first-person plural past tense of Proto-Turkic *kīr- (“to enter”) or *kïr- (“to break”).

Related to Polish przekobiały. Originally referred to animal skin that has cross (пер-ко-) white (белый) lines. An archaic phrase: "Чёрного кобеля не отмоешь добела" meant that black dog (or another animal) with cross-white lines on its skin can't be washed to whiteness. Related to adjective Russian

parole.significato: tail fat, fat tail (of a sheep)

parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yakšï (“good”). Compare Tatar яхшы (yaxşı), Crimean Tatar yahşı, Azerbaijani yaxşı.

Attested since the 17th century. Borrowed from a Turkic source. Ultimately, from Proto-Turkic *tuman (“mist, fog”), or from Avestan 𐬛𐬎𐬥𐬨𐬀𐬥 (dunman, “fog, mist”), 𐬛𐬎𐬎𐬄𐬥𐬨𐬀𐬥 (duuąnman, “cloud”), from Proto-Iranian *dʰuHmás, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *dʰuHmás.
